name: Architectural Concept Design Presentation
description: A competition-ready architectural concept presentation moving from project brief and site reading through concept derivation, spatial program, material and sustainability strategy, key renders, and design-stage summary.
style_guide:
# Architectural Concept Design Presentation

## Design intent

Create a rigorous architectural narrative in which form emerges visibly from context, program, climate, material, and public purpose. The sequence should establish the brief, interpret the site, derive the organizing idea, test areas and adjacencies, explain structure and envelope, quantify environmental intent, and close with renders that synthesize—not replace—the evidence. Warm drawing-paper pages support plans and diagrams; charcoal fields hold the civic thesis; copper orange marks site, movement, and decisions; timber and brick tones connect diagrams to material reality.

The previews provide visual grammar only. Do not copy their architect, client, project, site, city, brief, dimensions, areas, budget, program, concept, materials, carbon targets, certifications, dates, renders, or design claims. Build every element from current project evidence.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `48–60 px` side margins, `28–36 px` top framing, and a fine project footer.
- Use a 12-column grid with `16–20 px` gutters. Align site plans, diagram frames, program totals, adjacency matrices, material boards, performance bars, render crops, captions, and scales.
- Reserve `95–130 px` for a section code, conclusion-led title, and one technical framing sentence.
- Prefer one primary drawing or render with one supporting analytical region. Avoid tiling many small images without hierarchy.
- Use square frames, thin rules, no shadow, and precise alignment. White space should evoke a drawing set while remaining legible in presentation format.

## Color system

- Drawing ivory: `#F4EFE5` for plans, analysis, schedules, and technical content.
- Studio charcoal: `#191918` for the project thesis, concept sequence, selected rooms, and high-contrast captions.
- Copper orange: `#C85B2D` for the site boundary, paths, program emphasis, annotations, milestones, and key environmental values.
- Timber brown: `#9A6A3A` for material identity, warmth, and selected interior elements.
- Concrete gray: `#B8B2A8` for existing context, secondary geometry, baselines, and technical grids.
- Orange must indicate the proposal or design move; gray represents context or reference. Never reverse those semantics between pages.

## Typography

- Use `Inter`, `Aptos`, `Helvetica Neue`, or another precise modern sans-serif.
- Cover title: `54–70 px`; page headline: `34–44 px`; technical body: `11–14 px`; program and performance tables: `9–12 px`; captions and drawing metadata: `8–10 px`.
- A restrained italic may emphasize the design action or spatial quality within a title.
- Use uppercase tracking for section codes, drawing titles, stage, status, scale, and revision metadata.
- Use tabular numerals and unambiguous units for area, length, capacity, energy, carbon, cost, dates, and scale.

## Drawings, diagrams, and components

- Every plan, section, elevation, and site drawing needs a title, scale or `NTS`, north point where relevant, legend, revision, date, and source.
- Site analysis should distinguish existing conditions, measured observations, regulatory constraints, and design interpretation.
- Concept sequences should show no more than four meaningful transformations from context to form, each with a short causal statement.
- Program schedules must reconcile gross and net area, floor, use, capacity, circulation, support, and total.
- Adjacency diagrams should define essential, direct, desirable, and indirect relationships with labels beyond color alone.
- Material boards need application, finish, performance, sourcing status, maintenance, fire, weathering, and sample status.
- Sustainability bars must show baseline, target, method, boundary, design stage, and verification status.
- Render pages should caption viewpoint, status, principal design move, and the evidence still requiring development.

## Page families

### Architectural cover

Use a single full-bleed project render or current-site image with a dark atmospheric grade. Include project, location, client, architect, presentation stage, revision, date, status, and one sentence defining the concept question.

### Project context and design brief

Use a dark thesis panel beside five or fewer numbered brief moves. Translate client requirements and constraints into explicit spatial, structural, environmental, schedule, and budget criteria.

### Site analysis and concept derivation

Pair a legible site plan with four site findings and a compact transformation sequence. Show how access, solar, wind, heritage, views, topography, ecology, flood, noise, or urban grain actually influence form.

### Spatial program and organization

Combine a key plan with area and capacity totals, distribution bars, and an adjacency matrix. Keep program names and totals consistent with the brief and source schedule.

### Materials, facade, and sustainability

Pair a facade or assembly study with a concise material board and quantified performance targets. Distinguish aesthetic intention from specified product and verified result.

### Key renders and design summary

Use one dominant interior or public-space render with two supporting views. Close on a compact strip summarizing civic value, program, environmental ambition, design stage, and next validation step.

## Imagery and representation

- Use current drawings, measured surveys, physical or digital models, verified context photography, and clearly labelled concept renders.
- Maintain consistent material color, sun direction, season, occupancy assumptions, and design stage across views.
- Show people only to communicate scale and use; do not imply demographic or operational certainty.
- Label AI-assisted, composited, outsourced, or illustrative imagery where applicable. A render is not evidence of constructability or approval.

## Content integrity and technical truth

- Do not invent client requirements, site facts, surveys, zoning, ownership, heritage status, flood level, climate data, program, area, capacity, cost, schedule, materials, structural system, performance, approval, or certification.
- Distinguish existing, surveyed, client-provided, inferred, proposed, optioned, coordinated, approved, tendered, and as-built information.
- Preserve drawing revisions, coordinate system, units, scales, authorship, consultant source, and evidence dates.
- Reconcile area totals across brief, plan, schedule, occupancy, cost, and sustainability calculations.
- Carbon, energy, daylight, water, biodiversity, and certification claims require stated methodology, system boundary, baseline, model stage, assumptions, and responsible consultant.
- Verify structure, envelope, fire safety, accessibility, egress, acoustics, services, planning, heritage, landscape, and cost with the relevant disciplines.
- Do not present a concept-stage detail as technically resolved or a target as achieved performance.
- Protect confidential site, security, procurement, cost, and client information according to presentation audience.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview projects, sites, client briefs, areas, capacities, materials, diagrams, targets, renderings, budgets, or dates.
- Do not let a cinematic render replace site evidence, program reconciliation, technical coordination, or risk.
- Do not use arbitrary arrows, unexplained bubbles, decorative plans, false precision, or diagrams without legends.
- Do not hide unresolved access, fire, structure, servicing, planning, cost, or environmental dependencies.
- Do not use glass cards, heavy shadows, glossy gradients, 3D charts, generic architecture icons, or illegible drawing notes.
